Nickel(II)-Catalyzed [3 + 2] Cycloaddition of Nitrones and Allenoates
to Access N‑Vinylindoles and N‑Vinylpyrroles
Pei-Pei Xu, § Jun-Yi Liao, § Jia-Jie Zhang, Wei-Min Shi, * Cui Liang, Gui-Fa Su, * and Dong-Liang Mo *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 7482 −7486 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A variety of N-vinylindoles and N-vinylpyrroles
were prepared in moderate to good yields through the nickel(II)-
catalyzed [3 + 2] cycloaddition of α,β-unsaturated nitrones with
allenoates under mild reaction conditions. A rational mechanism
for the formation of N-vinylindoles was proposed based on the
18O-labeled experiments and key intermediates detected by high-
resolution mass spectrometry trace experiments. The present
method highlights a nickel(II)-co ntrolled cyclization, atom-
economical reaction, broad substrate scope, good functional
group tolerance, and high Z-stereoselectivity for the enamine bond.
N-Vinylindole derivatives not only are extensively found as
core structures in various natural products and pharmaceut-
icals, such as apovincamine and apotacamine,
1 but also widely
serve as valuable intermediates in various reactions or
monomers for photoactive and polymeric materials.
2 Many
strategies for the synthesis of N-vinylindoles have been
developed in the past decades, including the stereospeci ﬁc
Pd-catalyzed N-vinylation of indoles with vinyl tri ﬂates or vinyl
halides,3 Pd-catalyzed oxidative cross-coupling of indoles and
alkenes,4 condensation of indoles with ketones, 5 intermolecular
addition of indoles to alkynes, 6 Pd-catalyzed coupling of N −H
indoles with N-tosylhydrazones, 7 and cyclization of o-
alkynylaniline derivatives. 8 However, these reactions have
usually suﬀered low eﬃciency and required a high temperature,
expensive transition-metal catalysts, or strict reaction con-
ditions. Hence, the development of new strategies toward the
synthesis of N-vinylindoles from easily available starting
materials and inexpensive metal catalysts is valuable.
Nitrones, serving as important 1,3-dipoles, have been one of
the most attractive building blocks for building indole sca ﬀolds
or other heterocycles.9 In the last two decades, α,β-unsaturated
nitrones have attracted great attention in the preparation of
complex target molecules owing to the rich transformations of
the α,β-unsaturated bonds in nitrones during their reaction
with other dipolarphiles. 10 In particular, the cycloaddition of
α,β-unsaturated nitrones with allenoates was investigated. 11
For example, in 1999, Ishar and coworkers developed the
reaction of benzopyranone nitrone and allenoate to access
benzoindolizines through a metal-free cascade of a [3 + 2]
cycloaddition/[3,3]-rearrangement/retro-Mannich reaction/
Diels−Alder reaction ( Scheme 1 A).12 In 2014, Anderson and
coworkers pioneered a metal-free solvent-controlled strategy to
prepare dihydrocarbazoles and dihydropyridoindoles, respec-
tively, from N-aryl-α,β-unsaturated nitrones and unsubstituted
allenoates ( Scheme 1 B).13 Later, an asymmetric synthesis of
dihydropyridoindoles was achieved through a bifunctional
thiourea catalyst.

enaminoketones was reported by the [3,3]-rearrangement of
dialkenylhydroxylamines through N-vinylﬂuorenyl nitrones
with monosubstituted allenoates. 15 The key intermediate for
these strategies was benzoazepine, which has illustrated
appealing versatility for the synthesis of indole derivatives by
further transformations. In 2020, we developed a commercial
gimeracil-catalyzed formal [4 + 1] cycloaddition of N-
vinylﬂuorenyl nitrones with allenoates to prepare a series of
spiroﬂuorenylpyrrolines in good yields, showing that allenoates
serve as a one-carbon synthon for the ring formation.
16 During
the study of the [3 + 2] cycloaddition of α,β-unsaturated
nitrones with various dipolarphiles in our group, 17 we surmised
that metal catalysts, such as the inexpensive nickel(II) catalyst,
might control a new transformation of benzoazepine
intermediates owing to the easy coordination to the dicarbonyl
group of benzoazepine. Herein we report that α,β-unsaturated
nitrones reacted with allenoates, a ﬀording N-vinylindoles and
N-vinylpyrroles in the presence of a nickel(II) catalyst under
mild reaction conditions through a cascade of [3 + 2]
cycloaddition, [3,3]-rearrangement, retro-Mannich reaction,
condensation, and 1,4-addition in a one-pot reaction ( Scheme
1C).
Initially, nitrone 1a and allenoate 2a were chosen as model
substrates to explore the optimal reaction conditions. As
shown in Table 1 , nitrone 1a reacted with allenoate 2a in
toluene at room temperature for 24 h, a ﬀording the desired N-
vinylindole 3aa in 26% yield with 1:1 Z/E isomers for the
enamine bond ( Table 1 , entry 1). Solvent screening showed
that dichloromethane (DCM) gave a higher yield than
tetrahydrofuran (THF) and dichloroethane (DCE), and 3aa
was not observed in acetonitrile (MeCN) or dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO) ( Table 1 , entries 2 −6). Adding Lewis acid catalysts,
such as FeCl
3 and ZnCl 2, delivered 3aa in 28 and 40% yield,
respectively ( Table 1 , entries 7 and 8). These results showed
that adding a Lewis acid catalyst completely improved the Z/E
ratio of 3aa. Pleasingly, NiCl
2 as a catalyst improved the yield
of 3aa to 65% with a Z isomer only, which was determined by
its 2D nuclear Overhauser e ﬀect spectroscopy (NOESY)
spectra (Table 1, entry 9). The in ﬂuence of N-ligands was also
evaluated ( Table 1 , entries 10 −13). The addition of 2,2-
bipyridine ( L1) and 1,10-phenanthroline ( L2)o b v i o u s l y
improved product 3aa to 81 and 74% yield, respectively,
whereas 2,9-dimethyl-1,10-phenanthroline ( L3) and Pybox
(L4) did not improve the yield, but the Z/E ratio of the
enamine bond remained as 20:1. These results showed a higher
reactivity of L1 and L2 than those using L3 and L4, perhaps
owing to the steric e ﬀect. The addition of MgSO
4 as an
additive to the standard conditions a ﬀorded 3aa in 83% yield
(Table 1 , entry 14). However, adding NaOH completely
prohibited the formation of 3aa (Table 1, entry 15). Therefore,
the optimal conditions for preparing 3aa were NiCl 2 (20 mol
%), L1 (24 mol %) as a ligand, and MgSO 4 as an additive in
DCM at room temperature (rt).
With the optimized conditions in hand, we then explored
the reaction scope with a variety of α,β-unsaturated nitrones 1
(Scheme 2 ). Various dibenzylideneacetone-derived nitrones
1a−1h with electron-donating and electron-withdrawing
groups at the para, meta, and ortho positions of the aryl ring
smoothly a ﬀorded the corresponding products 3aa−3ha in
good yields. When 1.0 g of nitrone 1a (3 mmol) was carried
out under the standard conditions, 3aa was obtained in 67%
yield. Nitrone 1i tolerated a 2-thienyl heteroaryl group,
delivering 3ia in 59% yield. Chalcone-derived nitrones 1j

with a phenyl and 1k with a styrenyl at the R 2 group both
reacted with 2a, smoothly a ﬀording 3ja and 3ka in 47 and 67%
yield, respectively. In addition to α,β-unsaturated ketone
moieties, N-aryl groups were also evaluated. The substituents
of N-aryl moieties could be present with electron-donating and
electron-withdrawing groups at the para, meta, and ortho
positions of the aryl ring, such as thioether, vinyl, halide, and
ester groups, giving the corresponding products 3la−3ua in
moderate to good yields. When the R
3 of nitrone 1s was a
methyl group at the meta position, the [3,3]-rearrangement
regioselectivity was 1.5/1. Pleasingly, nitrone 1v with 2-
naphthalenyl furnished 3va in 73% yield as a single isomer with
high [3,3]-rearrangement regioselectivity. When carbazole-
derived nitrones 1w and 1x were carried out under the
standard conditions, products 3wa and 3xa were obtained in
84 and 63% yield, respectively.
Next, the scope of allenoates was also studied. As shown in
Scheme 3 , a variety of allenoates 2 smoothly reacted with
nitrone 1a to a ﬀord the corresponding products 3ab−3an in
moderate to good yields ranging from 18 to 79%. The R group
of allenoate could be present with alkyl, aryl, and alkenyl
groups. When the R group was i-Pr or t-Bu, the yields of 3ad
and 3ae dropped to 57 and 31% yield, respectively. These
results indicated that the steric e ﬀect of the R group had a
great impact on the yield of N-vinyl indoles. The R
4 group of
allenoate was also evaluated. Interestingly, when unsubstituted
allenoate 2h was carried out under the standard conditions, N-
vinylindole 3ah was also obtained in 42% yield, and the
corresponding dihydrocarbaz ole and dihydropyridoindole
scaﬀolds reported in Anderson ’s method were not observed
in this case. The i-Pr-, t-Bu-, and Ph-substituted allenoates
(2k−2m) all gave lower yields ( 3ak−3am). These exper-
imental results demonstrated that the steric hindrance of R
4
had a signi ﬁcant e ﬀect on the formation of N-vinylindoles.
When a (−)-menthol derived allenoate 2n was subjected to the
standard conditions, product 3an was obtained in 35% yield
with a 1:1 diastereoselectivity.
In addition to N-aryl nitrones, N-vinyl nitrones were also
tested with 2a to determine the reaction compatibility. As
shown in Scheme 4 , it was found that various N-vinyl-α,β-
unsaturated nitrones 4a−4f and allenoates ( 2a, 2b, 2f, 2g)
proceeded smoothly to a ﬀord the corresponding polysub-
stituted N-vinylpyrroles 5aa−5ag in moderate yields. In these
cases, the yields of N-vinylpyrroles were lower than those of N-
vinylindoles because of the easy decomposition of N-vinyl
nitrones to the corresponding ketones in the presence of a
nickel(II) catalyst. This met hod provides an alternative
approach to the preparation of polysubstituted N-vinylpyrroles.
On the basis of the O
18-labeled experimental results
suggesting that the hydroxyl group in 3aa might be derived
from water and the detection of intermediates by high-
resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) trace experiments,
18 a
possible mechanism for the formation of N-vinylindole 3aa
from 1a and 2a was proposed ( Scheme 5). Initially, the NiCl 2·
L1 complex was immediately formed when NiCl 2 was mixed
with L1.19 Then, nitrone 1a was activated by the NiCl 2·L1
catalyst and underwent a [3 + 2] cycloaddition with allenoate
2a to form intermediate A. A [3,3]-rearrangement of A
aﬀorded benzoazepine B, which underwent a retro-Mannich
reaction and enolation of the 1,3-dicarbonyl group in the
presence of NiCl
2·L1 to give imine C and HCl. Imine C
underwent an intramolecular aza-Michael addition activated by
Ni(II) to form D. Intermediate D went through an elimination
and was trapped by HCl to form indole sca ﬀold E, which was

Supporting Information .) Intermediate E facilitated an intra-
molecular 1,4-addition from one side of the styrenyl to give N-
vinylindole 3aa with high Z-selectivity of the enamine bond
owing to the carbonyl group serving as a directing group and
ﬁnally released the Ni(II) ·L1 catalyst to ﬁnish the catalytic
cycle.
In summary, we have identi ﬁed a nickel(II)-catalyzed [3 +
2] cycloaddition of α,β-unsaturated nitrones with allenoates to
prepare a variety of N-vinylindoles and N-vinylpyrroles in
moderate to good yields under mild reaction conditions. The
reaction tolerated diverse nitrones and allenoates with various
functional groups. Mechanistic studies revealed that the
nickel(II) catalyst played an important role in the reaction
selectivity. This method features mild reaction conditions, a
broad substrate scope, a highly atom-economical reaction, and
high Z-selectivity of the enamine bond.

Nickel(II)-Catalyzed [3 + 2] Cycloaddition of Nitrones and Allenoates
to Access N‑Vinylindoles and N‑Vinylpyrroles
Pei-Pei Xu, § Jun-Yi Liao, § Jia-Jie Zhang, Wei-Min Shi, * Cui Liang, Gui-Fa Su, * and Dong-Liang Mo *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 7482 −7486 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A variety of N-vinylindoles and N-vinylpyrroles
were prepared in moderate to good yields through the nickel(II)-
catalyzed [3 + 2] cycloaddition of α,β-unsaturated nitrones with
allenoates under mild reaction conditions. A rational mechanism
for the formation of N-vinylindoles was proposed based on the
18O-labeled experiments and key intermediates detected by high-
resolution mass spectrometry trace experiments. The present
method highlights a nickel(II)-co ntrolled cyclization, atom-
economical reaction, broad substrate scope, good functional
group tolerance, and high Z-stereoselectivity for the enamine bond.
N-Vinylindole derivatives not only are extensively found as
core structures in various natural products and pharmaceut-
icals, such as apovincamine and apotacamine,
1 but also widely
serve as valuable intermediates in various reactions or
monomers for photoactive and polymeric materials.
2 Many
strategies for the synthesis of N-vinylindoles have been
developed in the past decades, including the stereospeci ﬁc
Pd-catalyzed N-vinylation of indoles with vinyl tri ﬂates or vinyl
halides,3 Pd-catalyzed oxidative cross-coupling of indoles and
alkenes,4 condensation of indoles with ketones, 5 intermolecular
addition of indoles to alkynes, 6 Pd-catalyzed coupling of N −H
indoles with N-tosylhydrazones, 7 and cyclization of o-
alkynylaniline derivatives. 8 However, these reactions have
usually suﬀered low eﬃciency and required a high temperature,
expensive transition-metal catalysts, or strict reaction con-
ditions. Hence, the development of new strategies toward the
synthesis of N-vinylindoles from easily available starting
materials and inexpensive metal catalysts is valuable.
Nitrones, serving as important 1,3-dipoles, have been one of
the most attractive building blocks for building indole sca ﬀolds
or other heterocycles.9 In the last two decades, α,β-unsaturated
nitrones have attracted great attention in the preparation of
complex target molecules owing to the rich transformations of
the α,β-unsaturated bonds in nitrones during their reaction
with other dipolarphiles. 10 In particular, the cycloaddition of
α,β-unsaturated nitrones with allenoates was investigated. 11
For example, in 1999, Ishar and coworkers developed the
reaction of benzopyranone nitrone and allenoate to access
benzoindolizines through a metal-free cascade of a [3 + 2]
cycloaddition/[3,3]-rearrangement/retro-Mannich reaction/
Diels−Alder reaction ( Scheme 1 A).12 In 2014, Anderson and
coworkers pioneered a metal-free solvent-controlled strategy to
prepare dihydrocarbazoles and dihydropyridoindoles, respec-
tively, from N-aryl-α,β-unsaturated nitrones and unsubstituted
allenoates ( Scheme 1 B).13 Later, an asymmetric synthesis of
dihydropyridoindoles was achieved through a bifunctional
thiourea catalyst.

enaminoketones was reported by the [3,3]-rearrangement of
dialkenylhydroxylamines through N-vinylﬂuorenyl nitrones
with monosubstituted allenoates. 15 The key intermediate for
these strategies was benzoazepine, which has illustrated
appealing versatility for the synthesis of indole derivatives by
further transformations. In 2020, we developed a commercial
gimeracil-catalyzed formal [4 + 1] cycloaddition of N-
vinylﬂuorenyl nitrones with allenoates to prepare a series of
spiroﬂuorenylpyrrolines in good yields, showing that allenoates
serve as a one-carbon synthon for the ring formation.
16 During
the study of the [3 + 2] cycloaddition of α,β-unsaturated
nitrones with various dipolarphiles in our group, 17 we surmised
that metal catalysts, such as the inexpensive nickel(II) catalyst,
might control a new transformation of benzoazepine
intermediates owing to the easy coordination to the dicarbonyl
group of benzoazepine. Herein we report that α,β-unsaturated
nitrones reacted with allenoates, a ﬀording N-vinylindoles and
N-vinylpyrroles in the presence of a nickel(II) catalyst under
mild reaction conditions through a cascade of [3 + 2]
cycloaddition, [3,3]-rearrangement, retro-Mannich reaction,
condensation, and 1,4-addition in a one-pot reaction ( Scheme
1C).
Initially, nitrone 1a and allenoate 2a were chosen as model
substrates to explore the optimal reaction conditions. As
shown in Table 1 , nitrone 1a reacted with allenoate 2a in
toluene at room temperature for 24 h, a ﬀording the desired N-
vinylindole 3aa in 26% yield with 1:1 Z/E isomers for the
enamine bond ( Table 1 , entry 1). Solvent screening showed
that dichloromethane (DCM) gave a higher yield than
tetrahydrofuran (THF) and dichloroethane (DCE), and 3aa
was not observed in acetonitrile (MeCN) or dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO) ( Table 1 , entries 2 −6). Adding Lewis acid catalysts,
such as FeCl
3 and ZnCl 2, delivered 3aa in 28 and 40% yield,
respectively ( Table 1 , entries 7 and 8). These results showed
that adding a Lewis acid catalyst completely improved the Z/E
ratio of 3aa. Pleasingly, NiCl
2 as a catalyst improved the yield
of 3aa to 65% with a Z isomer only, which was determined by
its 2D nuclear Overhauser e ﬀect spectroscopy (NOESY)
spectra (Table 1, entry 9). The in ﬂuence of N-ligands was also
evaluated ( Table 1 , entries 10 −13). The addition of 2,2-
bipyridine ( L1) and 1,10-phenanthroline ( L2)o b v i o u s l y
improved product 3aa to 81 and 74% yield, respectively,
whereas 2,9-dimethyl-1,10-phenanthroline ( L3) and Pybox
(L4) did not improve the yield, but the Z/E ratio of the
enamine bond remained as 20:1. These results showed a higher
reactivity of L1 and L2 than those using L3 and L4, perhaps
owing to the steric e ﬀect. The addition of MgSO
4 as an
additive to the standard conditions a ﬀorded 3aa in 83% yield
(Table 1 , entry 14). However, adding NaOH completely
prohibited the formation of 3aa (Table 1, entry 15). Therefore,
the optimal conditions for preparing 3aa were NiCl 2 (20 mol
%), L1 (24 mol %) as a ligand, and MgSO 4 as an additive in
DCM at room temperature (rt).
With the optimized conditions in hand, we then explored
the reaction scope with a variety of α,β-unsaturated nitrones 1
(Scheme 2 ). Various dibenzylideneacetone-derived nitrones
1a−1h with electron-donating and electron-withdrawing
groups at the para, meta, and ortho positions of the aryl ring
smoothly a ﬀorded the corresponding products 3aa−3ha in
good yields. When 1.0 g of nitrone 1a (3 mmol) was carried
out under the standard conditions, 3aa was obtained in 67%
yield. Nitrone 1i tolerated a 2-thienyl heteroaryl group,
delivering 3ia in 59% yield. Chalcone-derived nitrones 1j

reacted with 2a, smoothly a ﬀording 3ja and 3ka in 47 and 67%
yield, respectively. In addition to α,β-unsaturated ketone
moieties, N-aryl groups were also evaluated. The substituents
of N-aryl moieties could be present with electron-donating and
electron-withdrawing groups at the para, meta, and ortho
positions of the aryl ring, such as thioether, vinyl, halide, and
ester groups, giving the corresponding products 3la−3ua in
moderate to good yields. When the R
3 of nitrone 1s was a
methyl group at the meta position, the [3,3]-rearrangement
regioselectivity was 1.5/1. Pleasingly, nitrone 1v with 2-
naphthalenyl furnished 3va in 73% yield as a single isomer with
high [3,3]-rearrangement regioselectivity. When carbazole-
derived nitrones 1w and 1x were carried out under the
standard conditions, products 3wa and 3xa were obtained in
84 and 63% yield, respectively.
Next, the scope of allenoates was also studied. As shown in
Scheme 3 , a variety of allenoates 2 smoothly reacted with
nitrone 1a to a ﬀord the corresponding products 3ab−3an in
moderate to good yields ranging from 18 to 79%. The R group
of allenoate could be present with alkyl, aryl, and alkenyl
groups. When the R group was i-Pr or t-Bu, the yields of 3ad
and 3ae dropped to 57 and 31% yield, respectively. These
results indicated that the steric e ﬀect of the R group had a
great impact on the yield of N-vinyl indoles. The R
4 group of
allenoate was also evaluated. Interestingly, when unsubstituted
allenoate 2h was carried out under the standard conditions, N-
vinylindole 3ah was also obtained in 42% yield, and the
corresponding dihydrocarbaz ole and dihydropyridoindole
scaﬀolds reported in Anderson ’s method were not observed
in this case. The i-Pr-, t-Bu-, and Ph-substituted allenoates
(2k−2m) all gave lower yields ( 3ak−3am). These exper-
imental results demonstrated that the steric hindrance of R
4
had a signi ﬁcant e ﬀect on the formation of N-vinylindoles.
When a (−)-menthol derived allenoate 2n was subjected to the
standard conditions, product 3an was obtained in 35% yield
with a 1:1 diastereoselectivity.
In addition to N-aryl nitrones, N-vinyl nitrones were also
tested with 2a to determine the reaction compatibility. As
shown in Scheme 4 , it was found that various N-vinyl-α,β-
unsaturated nitrones 4a−4f and allenoates ( 2a, 2b, 2f, 2g)
proceeded smoothly to a ﬀord the corresponding polysub-
stituted N-vinylpyrroles 5aa−5ag in moderate yields. In these
cases, the yields of N-vinylpyrroles were lower than those of N-
vinylindoles because of the easy decomposition of N-vinyl
nitrones to the corresponding ketones in the presence of a
nickel(II) catalyst. This met hod provides an alternative
approach to the preparation of polysubstituted N-vinylpyrroles.
On the basis of the O
18-labeled experimental results
suggesting that the hydroxyl group in 3aa might be derived
from water and the detection of intermediates by high-
resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) trace experiments,
18 a
possible mechanism for the formation of N-vinylindole 3aa
from 1a and 2a was proposed ( Scheme 5). Initially, the NiCl 2·
L1 complex was immediately formed when NiCl 2 was mixed
with L1.19 Then, nitrone 1a was activated by the NiCl 2·L1
catalyst and underwent a [3 + 2] cycloaddition with allenoate
2a to form intermediate A. A [3,3]-rearrangement of A
aﬀorded benzoazepine B, which underwent a retro-Mannich
reaction and enolation of the 1,3-dicarbonyl group in the
presence of NiCl
2·L1 to give imine C and HCl. Imine C
underwent an intramolecular aza-Michael addition activated by
Ni(II) to form D. Intermediate D went through an elimination
and was trapped by HCl to form indole sca ﬀold E, which was

In summary, we have identi ﬁed a nickel(II)-catalyzed [3 +
2] cycloaddition of α,β-unsaturated nitrones with allenoates to
prepare a variety of N-vinylindoles and N-vinylpyrroles in
moderate to good yields under mild reaction conditions. The
reaction tolerated diverse nitrones and allenoates with various
functional groups. Mechanistic studies revealed that the
nickel(II) catalyst played an important role in the reaction
selectivity. This method features mild reaction conditions, a
broad substrate scope, a highly atom-economical reaction, and
high Z-selectivity of the enamine bond.
